title: Periodic configurations in low-complexity two-dimensional shifts of finite type
formal: For every finite nonempty alphabet \(A\), finite nonempty shape \(D\subset\mathbb Z^2\), and set of allowed patterns \(P\subseteq A^D\) with \(|P|\leq|D|\), let \(X(D,P)=\{x:\mathbb Z^2\to A:\ (d\mapsto x(t+d))\in P\text{ for every }t\in\mathbb Z^2\}\). If \(X(D,P)\neq\varnothing\), must there exist \(x\in X(D,P)\) and a vector \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\) such that \(x(t+v)=x(t)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z^2\)?
why: This is a boundary question for how little local diversity can still enforce complete absence of global repetition. It links symbolic dynamics with the decidability of planar tiling constraints and isolates the arbitrary-shape obstruction beyond the established convex case.
status_note: The 2020 source explicitly conjectures periodic existence for arbitrary shapes, and its extended-version abstract continues to distinguish the convex result. A bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 did not locate a resolution of the arbitrary-shape statement. Recent crawl dates of the October 2020 talk were not treated as new research dates.

category_assignment.reason: The conjecture is a structural periodicity statement for finite-type symbolic languages, rather than a computability-degree comparison.

importance.reason: A substantial periodicity and tiling-decidability question with a sharp pattern-count threshold and a specific unresolved extension beyond convex shapes.

sentences: A finite list of local patterns defines all legal colorings of the integer plane.
The list is low-complexity when it has at most as many patterns as cells in its finite shape.
The question asks whether every nonempty such system admits at least one coloring with a nonzero translation period.
Rectangular and convex shapes are covered by the cited theorem, while arbitrary scattered shapes remain the stated target.
This asks for one periodic global coloring, rather than requiring every legal coloring to be periodic.

definitions: A configuration assigns one alphabet symbol to each lattice cell. A \(D\)-pattern is a function from \(D\) to \(A\), and distinct functions count as distinct patterns. The same allowed list \(P\) is enforced at every translate of \(D\); its entries need not all occur in a valid global configuration. The shape is arbitrary: it may be disconnected, nonconvex or contained in a proper sublattice. No rectangle, nearest-neighbor, connectedness or convexity assumption is imposed. A shift of finite type (SFT) is a set of configurations specified by finitely many forbidden finite patterns and all their translates. In the displayed presentation, the forbidden patterns are exactly \(A^D\setminus P\). The low-complexity restriction is on this finite allowed presentation, \(|P|\leq|D|\), not merely on the number of patterns observed in one chosen configuration. Periodic means invariant under at least one nonzero translation; two independent periods are not required in the proposition. An aperiodic SFT in the source’s terminology is nonempty and contains no configuration with even one nonzero period. All configurations and periods in the conclusion may depend on \(A,D,P\); no bound on a period’s size or running time of a construction is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every nonempty \(X(D,P)\) satisfying \(|P|\leq|D|\) contains a periodic configuration. Alternatively give explicit finite \(A,D,P\), prove the pattern-count bound and nonemptiness in Lean, and prove that every configuration in \(X(D,P)\) has no nonzero translation period. A nonperiodic member alone is not a counterexample, and a theorem restricted to convex shapes does not resolve the stated quantification.

context_blocks.text: A small set of local patterns can force large-scale regularity. If the shape consists of one cell, the bound permits at most one symbol, so every nonempty system is constant and periodic. Larger shapes can impose interacting constraints despite using at most as many allowed patterns as cells.

Kari and Moutot prove the implication for rectangular shapes in Corollary 5. Their conclusion extends the result to finite convex lattice shapes, meaning shapes containing all lattice points in their convex hull. The remaining question explicitly allows arbitrary shapes.

For the rectangular case, the existence of a periodic configuration also yields decidability of whether the finite local constraints admit any configuration; this is Corollary 6. General two-dimensional finite local constraints do not have this decidability property. The present card keeps periodic existence as its single main target.

Nivat’s conjecture makes a stronger demand about each individual configuration with few rectangular patterns: that configuration should itself be periodic. Here only one periodic member of the entire allowed system is required. An SFT can therefore satisfy this card even if it also has nonperiodic members.

The source describes why arbitrary scattered shapes are delicate. Such a shape may inspect only one parity class of lattice cells, allowing different sublattices to carry incompatible directions of periodicity. Known failures of an orbit-closure periodicity assertion for these shapes do not automatically supply a finite-type system with no periodic member.

The quantifier over all lattice cells matters. A collection of finite patches or a large computer-generated tiling does not by itself establish nonemptiness of an aperiodic SFT, nor does a search with no small period exclude every possible period.
